title: Downgrade attacks and crypto agility
summary: Attackers push both sides onto the weakest option they share. Refuse weak options, and design stored data so algorithms can be replaced.

steps.title: Downgrade attacks
body: When two parties **negotiate** (which TLS version, which cipher suite, which key size), an attacker in the middle can edit the offers so both sides settle on the **weakest** option they both still support, then break that.
- **POODLE** (2014): browsers retried failed connections with SSL 3.0, so an attacker forced failures and then broke SSL 3.0's CBC padding.
- **FREAK** and **Logjam** (2015): servers that still accepted 1990s "export-grade" 512-bit RSA or Diffie-Hellman could be tricked into using them.

Two defences, both built into TLS 1.3: **remove weak options entirely** (it has no export ciphers, no CBC, no RSA key exchange), and **authenticate the negotiation** (the server signs a hash of the whole handshake transcript, so edited offers are detected).

steps.prompt: A server supports TLS 1.3 and TLS 1.2 and, "for old clients", SSL 3.0. What does keeping SSL 3.0 do to its *modern* clients?
options: Exposes them too: an attacker can make the connection fall back to SSL 3.0 and attack that
Nothing: modern clients always use TLS 1.3
It only affects clients that request SSL 3.0 themselves
steps.explain: A protocol is as strong as the weakest option an attacker can force. Supporting a broken option is supporting it for everyone.

steps.prompt: Match each attack or defence to what it involves.
pairs: A forced fallback to SSL 3.0 and its CBC padding
Detecting edited offers after the fact
steps.explain: All three attacks relied on servers keeping a weak option "just in case".

steps.title: Negotiate without falling back
steps.prompt: Write `string? Negotiate(string[] clientOffers, string[] serverPreference)` that returns the **first** entry of `serverPreference` (strongest first) that the client also offers, but **never** one of `SSL3`, `TLS1.0` or `TLS1.1`, even if both sides list it. Return `null` when nothing acceptable is left: refusing to connect is the correct outcome, not falling back.
template: Dojo.Eq("server preference wins over client order", "TLS1.3", Negotiate(new[] { "TLS1.3", "TLS1.2" }, dojoServer));
Dojo.Eq("an old client gets 1.2", "TLS1.2", Negotiate(new[] { "TLS1.2", "TLS1.0" }, dojoServer));
Dojo.Eq("an attacker who strips everything but SSL3 gets nothing", (string?)null, Negotiate(new[] { "SSL3" }, dojoServer));
Dojo.Eq("TLS1.0 is refused even when both list it", (string?)null, Negotiate(new[] { "TLS1.0", "TLS1.1" }, dojoServer));
hints: Loop over `serverPreference`, not the client's list: the server decides the order.
Skip anything in the forbidden list before checking the client's offers.

steps.title: Crypto agility: label everything
body: Algorithms age: MD5, SHA-1, DES, RC4 and 1024-bit RSA were all standard once. **Crypto agility** means you can replace an algorithm without a flag day, and it starts with **storing which algorithm made each value**:

The reader dispatches on the label; the writer always uses the newest version; and old values are upgraded **when they are next used** (on login you have the password, so you can rehash it). The key-id prefixes from module 5 and the `alg` and `kid` headers of a JWT are the same idea. Data without a label can only be migrated by guessing.

steps.explain: The label says which algorithm, the next field its cost, then salt and hash. Everything a future version of your code needs to verify (or upgrade) the value is in the value.

steps.prompt: Order the steps to replace an algorithm in a live system.
lines: Add the new algorithm with its own version label, keeping the old one for reading
Write all new values with the new version
Upgrade old values as they are used (rehash on login, rewrap on read)
Run a background job for values nobody touches
Remove the old algorithm once no stored value uses it
also: Add the new algorithm with its own version label, keeping the old one for reading
Write all new values with the new version
Run a background job for values nobody touches
Upgrade old values as they are used (rehash on login, rewrap on read)
Remove the old algorithm once no stored value uses it
steps.explain: Read support first, then write, then migrate, and delete last. Lazy upgrades and the background job can run in either order.

steps.title: Versioned password hashes with upgrade on login
prompt: - `v1$<hex SHA-256 of the password>`: legacy, still readable.

Write `string HashV2(string password, byte[] salt, int iterations)` and `bool Verify(string stored, string password, out bool needsUpgrade)`. `needsUpgrade` is `true` when the password is correct **and** the value is v1 or uses fewer than `CurrentIterations`. Compare with `FixedTimeEquals`. Unknown labels return `false`.
`CurrentIterations` is tiny so the tests run fast; production PBKDF2-SHA256 uses about 600,000.
starter: string HashV2(string password, byte[] salt, int iterations)
bool Verify(string stored, string password, out bool needsUpgrade)
solution: string HashV2(string password, byte[] salt, int iterations)
var hash = Rfc2898DeriveBytes.Pbkdf2(password, salt, iterations, HashAlgorithmName.SHA256, 32);
bool Verify(string stored, string password, out bool needsUpgrade)
var hash = Rfc2898DeriveBytes.Pbkdf2(password, Convert.FromHexString(parts[2]), iterations, HashAlgorithmName.SHA256, 32);
template: var dojoV2 = HashV2("correct horse", dojoSalt, CurrentIterations);
Dojo.Check("HashV2 writes the v2 format", dojoV2.StartsWith("v2$2000$0102030405060708090a0b0c0d0e0f10$") && dojoV2.Length == 3 + 5 + 33 + 64, dojoV2);
Dojo.Check("a current v2 hash verifies with no upgrade", Verify(dojoV2, "correct horse", out var dojoU1) && !dojoU1, $"upgrade={dojoU1}");
Dojo.Check("a wrong password fails", !Verify(dojoV2, "wrong horse", out var dojoU2) && !dojoU2, "accepted a wrong password");
Dojo.Check("a legacy v1 hash verifies and asks for an upgrade", Verify(dojoV1, "correct horse", out var dojoU3) && dojoU3, $"upgrade={dojoU3}");
Dojo.Check("a wrong password on v1 asks for nothing", !Verify(dojoV1, "nope", out var dojoU4) && !dojoU4, "wrong result");
Dojo.Check("too few iterations asks for an upgrade", Verify(dojoWeak, "correct horse", out var dojoU5) && dojoU5, $"upgrade={dojoU5}");
Dojo.Check("an unknown label is refused", !Verify("v9$abc", "correct horse", out _), "accepted v9");
hints: `Rfc2898DeriveBytes.Pbkdf2(password, salt, iterations, HashAlgorithmName.SHA256, 32)` computes the v2 hash.
